label: Kinematics of Closed Chains
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 245 through 270 and shifts the mental model from composition to constraint. A closed chain forces several kinematic paths to agree on one body pose, so the configuration must live on the zero set of a loop equation rather than at the end of a single product of transforms.

label: From Open to Closed
notes: Open chains compose transforms forward and the joint vector freely chooses the pose. Closing the loop adds equations the joint values must jointly satisfy, dropping the mobility below the joint count. We name actuated and passive joints because only the actuated ones are commanded while the passive ones settle into an assembly.

label: Loop-Closure Constraints
notes: Loop closure writes the requirement that two paths reach the same frame as a vector equation in the joint coordinates. Stacking one equation per independent loop gives the constraint system whose solution set is the mechanism's configuration space, generally a curved implicit surface rather than a flat coordinate box.

label: Mobility by Counting
notes: Gruebler's formula estimates degrees of freedom from link and joint counts minus the constraints each joint imposes. It is a quick budget, not a guarantee: special geometries create overconstrained or paradoxically mobile linkages where the actual mobility differs from the count, so the formula is a first estimate to be checked against the constraint Jacobian.

label: Forward vs Inverse
notes: Parallel mechanisms invert the usual difficulty. Given a platform pose, each leg's required length or angle often follows from a direct geometric solve, making inverse kinematics easy. Going the other way, from actuator values to platform pose, can demand solving coupled polynomials with several real assembly modes, so forward kinematics is the harder problem.

label: The Planar Five-Bar
notes: The planar five-bar grounds two actuated revolute joints and joins them through three moving links to a shared end point. With two actuators and one loop it has two degrees of freedom. The same actuator pair can place the coupler point in distinct elbow configurations, the simplest example of multiple assembly modes.

label: The Stewart-Gough Platform
notes: The Stewart-Gough platform connects a fixed base to a moving platform through six legs whose lengths are the actuators. Inverse kinematics gives each length directly from the platform pose by a distance computation, while forward kinematics is famously hard, admitting up to forty assembly solutions for a general six-six geometry.

label: The Constraint Jacobian
notes: Differentiating the loop equation in time gives a linear relation between joint velocities through the constraint Jacobian. Splitting columns into actuated and passive parts yields two blocks. Allowed instantaneous motions are the null space of the full Jacobian, and the actuated block must be invertible to map commanded rates into platform velocity.

label: Three Kinds of Singularity
notes: Closed chains fail in three distinct ways. An actuator singularity makes the actuated Jacobian block drop rank, so commanded velocity cannot control the platform. An end-effector singularity lets the platform lose a freedom or resist a wrench for free. A configuration-space singularity is where assembly branches meet and the constraint surface stops being smooth.

label: Singular Geometry of the Loop
notes: Singularities have a geometric signature in the planar loop. When the elbow stretches fully or folds back, small changes in one coordinate stop producing independent endpoint motion and the Jacobian determinant crosses zero. The reach boundary and the fold curve mark where branches pinch together and conditioning degrades sharply near the surface.

label: Actuation and Branches
notes: An actuator vector alone does not pin down the configuration. The passive variables and the chosen branch complete it, and one actuator command can correspond to several physically distinct assemblies. Trajectory planning must therefore track which branch the mechanism occupies and avoid configuration-space singularities where an unintended branch switch could occur.

label: Recap and Takeaways
notes: Closed-chain kinematics is implicit geometry: configurations satisfy loop equations rather than a forward product. Inverse kinematics is usually easy and forward kinematics hard for parallel robots. The constraint Jacobian is the local diagnostic, and its rank loss flags the actuator, configuration-space, and end-effector singularities that bound safe operation.
